learn: Decision theory: decision regions, misclassification probability and the posterior rule
Why least squares fails for classification; linear discriminants
Sigmoid, logistic hypothesis, linear and non-linear boundaries
Cross-entropy cost, its convexity and its gradient; gradient descent
Confusion matrix metrics, class imbalance, ROC/AUC
intro.why: Logistic regression is the reference classifier: it is fast, interpretable and probabilistic, and it is a single neuron with a sigmoid (DNN Module 4). The evaluation tools here apply to every classifier.

symbols: joint density of input and class

sections.title: Decision theory: regions, mistakes and the posterior rule
sections.plain: Assign each x to the class with the largest posterior.
sections.body:
Target types: discrete $f(x)\in\{\text{Yes},\text{No}\}$ → classification; continuous → regression; probability estimation $f(x)\in[0,1]$. Running example: predict job offer from CGPA and IQ (IQ min-max normalised).

The central inference problem is learning $p(x,\mathcal C_k)$; then $$p(\mathcal C_k\mid x)=\frac{p(x\mid\mathcal C_k)p(\mathcal C_k)}{p(x)}=\frac{p(x,\mathcal C_k)}{\sum_{j}p(x,\mathcal C_j)}.$$ Stages: induction/inference (learn the model from training data) and deduction/decision (apply it to test data to choose an optimal threshold $t$).

Decision regions: the model divides input space into regions $\mathcal R_k$; all points in $\mathcal R_k$ get class $k$. Sample rule: IF CGPA < 7 THEN Job = 1 ELSE 0.

Misclassification rate: $$p(\text{mistake})=p(x\in\mathcal R_1,\mathcal C_2)+p(x\in\mathcal R_2,\mathcal C_1)=\int_{\mathcal R_1}p(x,\mathcal C_2)\,dx+\int_{\mathcal R_2}p(x,\mathcal C_1)\,dx.$$ To minimise it, put each $x$ in the class with the larger integrand: $p(x,\mathcal C_1)>p(x,\mathcal C_2)\iff p(\mathcal C_1\mid x)>p(\mathcal C_2\mid x)$, since $p(x)$ is common. Rule: choose the class with the largest posterior.

Summary: with boundary $\hat x$ the error is the red + green + blue area; moving to the optimal $x_0=\arg\min p(\text{mistake})$ (where the joint densities cross) removes the red area. The green and blue areas remain: this is the irreducible (Bayes) error.

sections.title: Generative vs discriminative models
sections.plain: Model each class, or model the boundary.
sections.body:
Generative: model $P(x\mid c)$ and $P(c)$, then use Bayes: $P(c\mid x)=\frac{P(x\mid c)P(c)}{P(x)}$; with conditional independence $P(c\mid X)\propto P(x_1\mid c)\cdots P(x_n\mid c)P(c)$. They can sample synthetic data. Examples: naïve Bayes (classification), Gaussian mixtures (clustering).

Discriminative: model the boundary or $P(c\mid x)$ directly, e.g. $\theta_0+\sum_i\theta_ix_i\ge0\Rightarrow y=1$. Examples: logistic regression, SVMs, decision trees (rules like IF CGPA > 6 AND IQ ≥ 7 THEN offer), neural networks, nearest neighbour.

sections.title: Least squares vs logistic regression; linear discriminants
sections.plain: Regression lines on 0/1 labels are fragile.
sections.body:
Least squares on 0/1 labels with rule "$h_\theta(x)\ge0.5\Rightarrow1$" works on a clean example, but adding one far-right positive tilts the line and misclassifies earlier points. On 2-D data extra points at the bottom-left drag the least-squares boundary badly while logistic regression barely moves: least squares is highly sensitive to outliers. Its outputs also lie outside [0, 1] (: $Y\in(-\infty,\infty)$).

Decision rule: linear discriminant $f(x,w)=w_0+w^\top x$ with $y=+1$ if $f\ge0$, else $-1$, i.e. $y=\operatorname{sign}(w_0+w^\top x)$.

sections.title: The sigmoid, logistic hypothesis and decision boundaries
sections.plain: Probability = sigmoid of a linear score.
sections.body:
We want $0\le h_\theta(x)\le1$: $$h_\theta(x)=g(\theta^\top x),\qquad g(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\ \Rightarrow\ h_\theta(x)=\frac1{1+e^{-\theta^\top x}}.$$ The model is linear in the log-odds: $\ln\frac{p}{1-p}=\theta_0+\sum_i\theta_ix_i$, the inverse of the sigmoid (the logit). Interpretation: $h_\theta(x)=0.7$ means a 70% chance of being selected.

Since $g(z)\ge0.5\iff z\ge0$, predict 1 iff $\theta^\top x\ge0$. Linear boundary: $\theta=(-3,1,1)$ gives $y=1$ iff $x_1+x_2\ge3$. Non-linear: with $h_\theta(x)=g(\theta_0+\theta_1x_1+\theta_2x_2+\theta_3x_1^2+\theta_4x_2^2)$ and $\theta=(-1,0,0,1,1)$, $y=1$ iff $x_1^2+x_2^2\ge1$ (outside the unit circle). Higher-order terms give more complex shapes.

Useful derivative: $g'(z)=g(z)(1-g(z))$.

sections.title: Cross-entropy cost and why not squared error
sections.plain: −log of the probability given to the true class.
sections.body:
Training set $\{(x^{(i)},y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^m$, $x_0=1$, $y\in\{0,1\}$. Plugging the sigmoid into squared error gives a non-convex $J(\theta)$ with local minima. Instead use:

$$\text{Cost}(h_\theta(x),y)=\begin{cases}-\log h_\theta(x)&y=1\\-\log(1-h_\theta(x))&y=0\end{cases}$$

If $y=1$: cost 0 when $h=1$, cost $\to\infty$ as $h\to0$ (we penalise confidently predicting no offer when there was one). Symmetric for $y=0$. Combined:

$$J(\theta)=-\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\left[y^{(i)}\log h_\theta(x^{(i)})+(1-y^{(i)})\log\left(1-h_\theta(x^{(i)})\right)\right].$$

Supplementary This is the negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli model $P(y\mid x)=h^y(1-h)^{1-y}$ (ML Module 8, MLE for logistic regression). Its Hessian $\frac1mX^\top SX$ with $S=\text{diag}(h_i(1-h_i))\succeq0$ shows $J$ is convex.

sections.title: Gradient of the cross-entropy and gradient descent
sections.plain: Same update as linear regression, different h.
sections.body:
Derivation. For one example, $\ell=-[y\log h+(1-y)\log(1-h)]$ with $h=g(z)$, $z=\theta^\top x$:

$$\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial h}=-\frac yh+\frac{1-y}{1-h}=\frac{h-y}{h(1-h)},\quad \frac{\partial h}{\partial z}=h(1-h),\quad \frac{\partial z}{\partial\theta_j}=x_j\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\theta_j}=(h-y)x_j.$$ $$\boxed{\frac{\partial J}{\partial\theta_j}=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\left(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\right)x_j^{(i)}},\qquad \theta_j\leftarrow\theta_j-\alpha\frac{\partial J}{\partial\theta_j}\ \text{(simultaneously)}.$$

The update looks identical to linear regression; only $h_\theta$ differs ($\theta^\top x$ vs $\frac1{1+e^{-\theta^\top x}}$). For the job example: $h_\theta(x)=\frac1{1+e^{-(\theta_0+\theta_1\text{CGPA}+\theta_2\text{IQ})}}$. Prediction for new $x$: output $h_\theta(x)$.

LOGISTIC-REGRESSION-GD(X, y, α, T)
  θ ← 0
  repeat T times
      h ← σ(X θ)                  # m probabilities
      g ← (1/m) Xᵀ (h − y)
      θ ← θ − α g
  return θ                          # predict 1 if σ(θᵀx) ≥ threshold

sections.title: Applications: sentiment and a worked fit
sections.body:
Sentiment with engineered features: $x_1$ = count of positive lexicon words (3), $x_2$ = negative (2), $x_3$ = 1 if "no" appears (1), $x_4$ = count of 1st/2nd-person pronouns (3), $x_5$ = 1 if "!" appears (0), $x_6=\ln(\text{word count})=\ln66=4.19$. With $w=[2.5,-5.0,-1.2,0.5,2.0,0.7]$, $b=0.1$: $$w\cdot x+b=7.5-10-1.2+1.5+0+2.933+0.1=0.833,\quad P(+\mid x)=\sigma(0.833)=0.70,\quad P(-\mid x)=0.30.$$

Fitting by gradient descent: six candidates (CGPA 5.5, 5, 8, 9, 6, 7.5; scaled IQ 6.7, 7, 6, 7, 8, 7.3; offers 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0), learning rate 0.3, initial weights (0.5, 0.5, 0.5), no regularisation. One step gives $\theta\approx(0.350,-0.424,-0.613)$ (computed below); the rounded result is (0.4, −0.4, −0.6).

Inference and interpretation: with $0.4+0.3\,\text{CGPA}-0.45\,\text{IQ}$ and candidate (5, 6): $z=-0.8$, $h=0.31$ → predict No. $e^{\theta_{CGPA}}=e^{0.3}=1.35$ is the odds ratio: each extra CGPA point multiplies the odds of an offer by 1.35 (in statsmodels: np.exp(model.params)).

sections.title: Regularisation for logistic regression
sections.plain: Penalise large weights; sklearn's C is the inverse strength.
sections.body: Identical in form to Module 3: $$\text{Loss}(S)=\sum_{i=1}^n\text{Loss}(\hat y_i,y_i)+\alpha\sum_j|\theta_j|\ \ (\text{L1})\quad\text{or}\quad+\tfrac\alpha2\sum_j\theta_j^2\ \ (\text{L2}).$$ In scikit-learn's LogisticRegression the strength is set by C, the inverse of α: larger C ⇒ weaker regularisation. Supplementary On linearly separable data the unregularised MLE does not exist (weights grow without bound); regularisation makes the solution finite.

sections.title: Confusion matrix and metrics
sections.body:
Predicted positivePredicted negative
Actual positivea = TPb = FN
Actual negativec = FPd = TN
$$\text{Accuracy}=\frac{a+d}{a+b+c+d},\quad \text{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\quad \text{Recall (TPR, sensitivity)}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}$$ $$\text{Specificity (TNR)}=\frac{TN}{TN+FP},\quad \text{FPR}=\alpha=\frac{FP}{TN+FP}=1-\text{spec.},\quad \text{FNR}=\beta=\frac{FN}{FN+TP}=1-\text{sens.},\quad \text{Power}=1-\beta$$ $$F_1=\frac{2\,\text{precision}\cdot\text{recall}}{\text{precision}+\text{recall}},\qquad \text{Error rate}=1-\text{accuracy}.$$

Accuracy is most effective with a balanced class distribution. Car-price example: 10 Low and 990 High cars; a model predicting everything "High" gets 990/1000 = 99% accuracy but detects none of the rare class. Model 1 (99%) vs Model 2 (50%, but catches the rare class): which is better depends on what matters.

sections.title: Which classifier is better? Effect of class skew
sections.plain: Precision collapses as negatives grow; recall and FPR don't.
sections.body:
Three classifiers keep the same recall and FPR as negatives grow 10× and 100×:

Skew (neg)T1 (TP 50, FN 50, FPR .01)T2 (TP 99, FN 1, FPR .1)T3 (TP 99, FN 1, FPR .01)
Low (100)p .98, F .66p .91, F .95p .99, F .99
Medium (1,000)p .83, F .62p .50, F .66p .91, F .95
High (10,000)p .33, F .40p .09, F .17p .50, F .66

Precision and F depend on class ratio; TPR and FPR do not. That is why ROC curves (TPR vs FPR) are insensitive to skew while precision-recall curves are not.

Which model?: Model 1 FPR 41%, FNR 3%; Model 2 FPR 5%, FNR 25%. Mistakes have different costs: disease screening needs low FNR (Model 1); spam filtering needs low FPR (Model 2). The same application may need different settings (conservative vs aggressive).

sections.title: ROC curves and AUC
sections.plain: TPR vs FPR across thresholds; area summarises ranking quality.
sections.body:
ROC (developed in the 1950s for signal detection) plots TPR against FPR. Landmarks: (0,0) everything negative; (1,1) everything positive; (0,1) ideal; diagonal = random guessing; below the diagonal = predictions opposite to truth. AUC = 1 for a perfect model, 0.5 for random; larger AUC is better for comparison. Uses: threshold selection, performance assessment, classifier comparison.

Example: 1-D data, points with $x>t$ classified positive; at threshold $t$: TPR 0.5, FNR 0.5, FPR 0.12, TNR 0.88.

Construction: score each instance, sort by decreasing score, apply a threshold at each unique score, count TP, FP, TN, FN, and plot TPR = TP/(TP+FN), FPR = FP/(FP+TN). Data: scores 0.95 (+), 0.93 (+), 0.87 (−), 0.85 (−), 0.85 (−), 0.85 (+), 0.76 (−), 0.53 (+), 0.43 (−), 0.25 (+). Points: (0,0), (0,.2), (0,.4), (.2,.4), (.6,.6), (.8,.6), (.8,.8), (1,.8), (1,1). AUC = 0.56.

Model comparison: no model may dominate. $M_1$ is better at small FPR, $M_2$ at large FPR; AUC summarises (ideal 1, random 0.5). Classic example: 10 tuples with probabilities 0.90…0.40 produce a step ROC curve.

Supplementary AUC equals the probability that a random positive is scored above a random negative (ties count ½).

sections.title: Class imbalance
sections.plain: Rare positives: resample, change the metric, or change the algorithm.
sections.body: The class of interest is often rare: fraud, cancer, or the minority outcome in the job example. Accuracy is then a poor metric. Solutions: generate synthetic samples from distances to nearest neighbours (SMOTE in imbalanced-learn); use recall, precision or ROC instead of accuracy; try algorithms that cope better (SVMs, tree-based methods). Supplementary Also: class_weight="balanced", threshold tuning on a validation set, and PR-AUC for heavily skewed data.

sections.title: Multi-class classification
sections.body:
Binary (spam/ham) vs multi-class (yes/no/maybe) outputs.

  • One-vs-rest: train $h_\theta^{(i)}(x)=P(y=i\mid x;\theta)$ for each class $i=1..K$; predict $\arg\max_ih_\theta^{(i)}(x)$. scikit-learn applies OvR automatically for binary classifiers (except SVMs, which use OvO).
  • One-vs-one: one classifier per pair, $N(N-1)/2$ in total; predict by voting / max.

Supplementary Multinomial (softmax) logistic regression models all classes jointly: $P(y=k\mid x)=\frac{e^{\theta_k^\top x}}{\sum_je^{\theta_j^\top x}}$ (see DNN Module 4).

Summary: model $h_\theta(x)=P(Y=1\mid X)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\theta^\top x}}$; cross-entropy cost; gradient descent; inference $\hat Y=h_\theta(x^{test})$. $\sigma(t)<0.5$ when $t<0$, so predict 1 iff $x^\top\theta\ge0$; logit$(p)=\log\frac p{1-p}$ is the inverse of the logistic function (the log-odds).

sections.title: Complexity, assumptions and comparisons
sections.body:
Cost: each GD iteration is $O(md)$; prediction $O(d)$. Second-order solvers (Newton/IRLS, L-BFGS) converge in few iterations at $O(md^2+d^3)$ per step.

Assumptions: log-odds linear in features (use basis functions otherwise); independent observations; little multicollinearity for stable coefficients; enough events per feature.

Logistic regressionNaïve Bayes (M8)Linear SVM (M7)Decision tree (M5)
TypeDiscriminative, probabilisticGenerativeDiscriminative, marginDiscriminative, rules
LossCross-entropyJoint likelihoodHingeImpurity
ProbabilitiesCalibrated-ishOften extremeNo (needs Platt scaling)Coarse
BoundaryLinear in featuresLinear/quadraticLinear (kernel for non-linear)Axis-aligned

sections.title: Common technical misconceptions
sections.body:
• "ROC is always the right curve." Under heavy imbalance, precision-recall curves reveal differences ROC hides.
  • "Coefficients are feature importances." Only after scaling, and only with low collinearity.
  • "Logistic regression outputs are well calibrated." Usually reasonable, but regularisation and resampling distort them.
  • "The decision boundary is where p = 0.5 regardless of threshold." Changing the threshold moves the operating boundary to $\theta^\top x=\text{logit}(t)$.
  • "Oversampling changes nothing but balance." It changes predicted probabilities; recalibrate or adjust the threshold.

code.title: One gradient-descent step and the reference examples
code.explain: Reproduces the job-offer GD step, the inference for candidate (5, 6) and the odds ratio, and the sentiment probability.
mistakes: Using unscaled features with a large learning rate: the first step overshoots, as here.
Forgetting the column of ones for θ0.
code.notes: In practice use scikit-learn's LogisticRegression (L-BFGS) and standardise features.
code.code:
import numpy as np

sig = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
#: 6 candidates, features CGPA and IQ (scaled column), label job offered
cgpa = np.array([5.5, 5, 8, 9, 6, 7.5]); iq = np.array([6.7, 7, 6, 7, 8, 7.3]); y = np.array([1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0])
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(6), cgpa, iq])

theta = np.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.5]); alpha = 0.3
h = sig(X @ theta)
grad = X.T @ (h - y) / len(y)             # (1/m) sum (h - y) x_j
print("h(x) before:", h.round(4))
print("gradient   :", grad.round(4))
print("theta after one step:", (theta - alpha * grad).round(4))

#: inference with theta = (0.4, 0.3, -0.45) for candidate (CGPA 5, IQ 6)
z = 0.4 + 0.3 * 5 - 0.45 * 6
print("h(5, 6) =", round(sig(z), 3), "-> predict", int(sig(z) >= 0.5))
print("odds ratio per +1 CGPA = e^0.3 =", round(np.exp(0.3), 2))

#: sentiment example
w = np.array([2.5, -5.0, -1.2, 0.5, 2.0, 0.7]); x = np.array([3, 2, 1, 3, 0, np.log(66)]); b = 0.1
print("P(+|x) =", round(sig(w @ x + b), 3), " w.x + b =", round(w @ x + b, 3))

code.title: Metrics under skew and the ROC example
code.explain: Recomputes precision, recall, FPR and F1 for the three classifiers at each skew level, and the ROC curve and AUC for the 10-instance example.
mistakes: Comparing precision across datasets with different class ratios.
code.notes: roc_curve merges tied scores into one threshold, matching the 'each unique value' rule.
code.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, roc_auc_score

def metrics(tp, fn, fp, tn):
    p, r, fpr = tp / (tp + fp), tp / (tp + fn), fp / (fp + tn)
    return dict(precision=round(p, 3), recall=round(r, 3), FPR=round(fpr, 3), F1=round(2 * p * r / (p + r), 3), accuracy=round((tp + tn) / (tp + fn + fp + tn), 3))

#: three classifiers under low / medium / high skew (rows: actual Yes, actual No)
cases = {"low":    [(50, 50, 1, 99), (99, 1, 10, 90), (99, 1, 1, 99)],
         "medium": [(50, 50, 10, 990), (99, 1, 100, 900), (99, 1, 10, 990)],
         "high":   [(50, 50, 100, 9900), (99, 1, 1000, 9000), (99, 1, 100, 9900)]}
for k, ts in cases.items():
    for i, t in enumerate(ts, 1): print(k, f"T{i}", metrics(*t))

#: ROC from 10 scored instances
score = np.array([0.95, 0.93, 0.87, 0.85, 0.85, 0.85, 0.76, 0.53, 0.43, 0.25])
label = np.array([1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1])
fpr, tpr, thr = roc_curve(label, score)
print("thresholds:", thr.round(2)); print("TPR:", tpr.round(2)); print("FPR:", fpr.round(2))
print("AUC =", round(roc_auc_score(label, score), 3))

code.title: Imbalanced data: plain vs class-weighted logistic regression
code.explain: With 5% positives, the plain model has high accuracy but low recall; class_weight='balanced' trades precision for recall at the 0.5 threshold.
mistakes: Tuning the threshold on the test set.
code.notes: Choose the threshold on validation data according to the business cost of FN vs FP.
code.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, roc_auc_score

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=4000, n_features=6, weights=[0.95], random_state=0)  # 5% positives
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, stratify=y, random_state=0)

for name, model in [("plain", LogisticRegression(C=1.0)), ("class_weight=balanced", LogisticRegression(C=1.0, class_weight="balanced"))]:
    model.fit(X_tr, y_tr); p = model.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
    print(f"--- {name}: AUC {roc_auc_score(y_te, p):.3f}")
    print(classification_report(y_te, (p >= 0.5).astype(int), digits=3, target_names=["neg", "pos"]))
